Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
The night of the mugging, Marcus had been walking back to his car after a late shift at the Coast Guard station in Astoria. It was just past eleven, the streets wet from earlier rain, and he was thinking about a maintenance log he'd forgotten to sign. He never saw the man until he was right in front of him, a knife catching the light from a streetlamp. What Marcus remembers now is not a story with a beginning, middle, and end. He remembers the glint of the blade, the cold pressure of the concrete against his cheek, the sound of his own breathing-too fast, too loud-and then the silence after the footsteps ran off. He cannot connect these pieces into a single narrative. When he tries to tell his girlfriend, Lauren, what happened, the words feel false, as if he is describing a scene from a movie. "I can't seem to put it into words," he told her once, and then stopped trying altogether. Sometimes, when a memory surfaces unbidden-the smell of wet asphalt, the weight of a hand on his shoulder-he observes it as if from a great distance, feeling nothing at all. It is as though the event happened to someone else, a stranger whose terror he can acknowledge but not inhabit. That numbness frightens him more than the flashbacks do.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself avoiding the neighborhood where it happened, taking a longer route to and from the station. At work, he began to volunteer for the overnight desk shifts, claiming he preferred the quiet. The truth was that the open, poorly lit pier where he used to run safety drills now made his stomach clench. His supervisor noticed he had stopped walking the perimeter alone during evening watch, something he had always done without thinking. Marcus told him it was nothing, just a preference. He did not explain that he now scanned every shadow twice, that his eyes tracked every pedestrian who walked too close to the chain-link fence. He had come to believe that danger was always lying in wait, that the world was simply a series of ambushes he had not yet seen coming. This hypervigilance was exhausting, but he was certain that letting his guard down even once would be a fatal mistake.

The consequences crept up on him. Lauren began to complain that he was distant, that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He started sleeping on the couch because her movements in bed made him feel trapped. At dinner, he would fall silent, his mind snagging on a flickering light or a sudden noise from the street. She asked him what was wrong, and he said he was tired. He could not tell her about the disconnected fragments that visited him at odd hours-the blade, the concrete, his own ragged breath-because they did not form a story he could share. He could not tell her that sometimes he felt nothing at all, and that this emptiness was worse than fear.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was not the memories themselves, but the growing distance between him and everything he cared about. He had started to feel like a ghost in his own life, watching himself go through the motions. Last week, during a routine inspection on the dock, a colleague clapped him on the back to get his attention. Marcus spun around, heart hammering, and shoved the man away before he could stop himself. The look of shock on his coworker's face was the same look he had seen on Lauren's face a dozen times. That night, he sat in his car in the driveway for an hour, trying to remember the drive home. He could not. The pieces of his day, like the pieces of that night, would not fit together. He is afraid that if he does not find a way to make them cohere, he will lose Lauren, lose his place in the unit, lose the person he used to be. He is afraid of what he might do the next time someone touches him without warning. But mostly, he is afraid that the numbness will spread, and that one day he will stop feeling anything at all.
